finding.claim: The /logo handler fetches an attacker-supplied URL. Its only check is strings.Contains(raw, "example.io"), which can be bypassed. The response body is streamed back to the caller, so this is full-read SSRF.
finding.sink: http.Get(raw) (main.go:36). It uses the default client, which follows redirects, and the response body is copied to the client (main.go:38).

trace.note: Only check is a substring match for "example.io" anywhere in the string. It does not parse the URL or check scheme, host or port.
http.Get(raw) is called with the unvalidated URL
The response body is returned to the attacker, so internal data is exfiltrated

finding.guards_checked: The only guard is the substring check at main.go:32. It is bypassed by http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/?x=example.io, http://example.io@127.0.0.1:8080/, or http://internal-host/#example.io. There is no scheme allowlist, no host parsing, no private/link-local IP blocking and no redirect restriction, because the default client follows redirects. Repro: curl 'http://host:8081/logo?logo=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/%3Fexample.io'. I checked /cdn (main.go:14-28) and did not report it. It parses the URL, does an exact Hostname() match against the trusted map and disables redirects, so the request can only reach cdn.example.io.

verdict.guard_found: Only strings.Contains(raw, "example.io") at main.go:32, a substring check that does not close the finding. There is no middleware, URL parsing, scheme check or redirect restriction on /logo.
verdict.reason: main.go:31 takes the attacker-controlled "logo" form value, main.go:32 only does a substring match that fails to block e.g. http://169.254.169.254/?example.io, and main.go:36 http.Get follows redirects and main.go:38 returns the body to the caller, so this is full-read SSRF.
